newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Porsche flush with profit, pride.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Porsche flush with profit, pride.

text.p: Porsche AG, flush with pride and cash, said on Friday that profit for the first half of its 1996-97 business year had more than trebled.
The German car maker also said it had signed a deal with Finland's Valmet Oy to help meet surging demand for the carmaker's popular Boxster roadster.

Porsche, proclaiming it was back in the fast lane after hard times and weak sales in the early 1990s, said profit rose to 36 million marks ($22 million) in the six-month period to January 31 from 10.3 million in the same 1995-96 period.
Sales jumped 20 percent to 1.7 billion marks as deliveries rose 25 percent to 12,800 vehicles, of which 3,150 were Boxsters, Porsche's first completely new car in two decades.

The six-month results prompted Porsche chief executive Wendelin Wiedeking to predict at the group's shareholder meeting that Porsche would top the 1995-96 business year sales of 2.8 billion marks and net profit of 48.1 million marks.
Shares in Porsche gained sharply on the results, advancing 140 marks to 1,510 marks in midday bourse dealings, a 10 percent gain that clearly outpaced the broader German market.
Porsche said demand for the two-seat roadster was so strong that it planned to crank up production in a deal with Valmet to build at least 5,000 of the vehicles from autumn 1997.
Demand is predicted to keep rising only as the Boxster is offered into new markets, including February in America where Porsche wants to double its 1997 sales to 14,000 vehicles.
The announcement confirmed media reports in Germany and Finland this week that Porsche was seeking a partner to reduce customer waiting times from the current level of one year.
"It will give us some room to breathe," Porsche spokesman Anton Hunger said about the deal with Valmet, noting the number of Boxsters to be produced in Finland may later be increased.

Porsche said production at its Stuttgart area plant was nearly exhausted since it has little scope to cut output of the more expensive 911 after sales boomed last year, prompting the need to find immediate production capacity with a partner.

But it stressed a commitment to maintaining jobs at its German plant and that the production at Valmet would create about 1,000 jobs at components suppliers in Germany, which account for about 80 percent of Boxster production.

Shareholders criticised Porsche leadership for the decision to seek foreign production help, particularly at a time of record unemployment in Germany, and told management to consider other German carmakers or creating new jobs at Porsche.

Porsche, saying it chose Valmet because of its excellent industry reputation, sought to calm fears by saying it would send Porsche workers to Finland to ensure that the cars will leave the plant with the "customary high Porsche quality".

Porsche also said it was committed to producing a sport-utility vehicle despite the breakdown of talks with Mercedes-Benz AG to develop an upscale market vehicle, seen as a bid by Porsche to break out of the sportscar market.
"We have decided that the Porsche brand would be well accepted" by customers considering whether to buy a sport-utility vehicle, Wiedeking said.
The talks ended because Porsche believed Mercedes wanted too strong an influence on the project, Wiedeking said.
"We have not lost substantial time with this project but instead have developed a lot of know-how that has created for us a good starting position," Wiedeking said.
The two carmakers started talks last summer to cooperate on making a top-end version of the Mercedes M-Class vehicle, set to begin production in the United States later this year.
Porsche officials said the car maker was now searching for a potential partner to develop a vehicle but said plans to introduce such a vehicle in 1999 were now rather unrealistic.
